title: Sampling Distribution of a Mean and the CLT
short: Sample means are close to normal for large n, with spread σ/√n.
trouble: Students think the central limit theorem makes the data themselves normal.

blocks.html: The same idea works for averages. Take many random samples, find each sample's mean $\bar{x}$, and look at how those means vary. The answer is one of the most important facts in statistics, the central limit theorem, and it parallels the sampling distribution of a proportion.

For random samples of size $n$ from a population with mean $\mu$ and SD $\sigma$: $$\mu_{\bar{x}} = \mu, \qquad \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}.$$ Central limit theorem: when $n$ is large, the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ is approximately normal, whatever the shape of the population. (If the population itself is normal, $\bar{x}$ is normal for every n.)

The sample total is a sum of $n$ independent values, so its mean is $n\mu$ and, because variances add, its variance is $n\sigma^2$. Dividing the total by $n$ gives $\bar{x}$: mean $\mu$ and variance $n\sigma^2/n^2 = \sigma^2/n$, so SD $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$. The normal shape is the deep part: when many independent pieces are averaged, high and low values offset each other, and the lopsidedness of any one value washes out. How large n must be depends on the skew; $n \ge 30$ is a common rule of thumb for moderately skewed populations.

blocks.name: sampling
blocks.cap: Start with n = 2 and add 1,000 samples: the means are still skewed. Slide n to 30: the means pile into a bell centered on μ, even though the population (top) is strongly skewed.

blocks.title: Center and spread
blocks.q: Commute times in a city are skewed right with mean 30 minutes and SD 12 minutes. For random samples of 36 workers, describe the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$.
steps: Shape: $n = 36$ is fairly large, so by the CLT $\bar{x}$ is approximately normal.

blocks.title: A probability about the mean
blocks.q: Find the probability that the mean commute of 36 workers is more than 33 minutes. ($P(Z < 1.50) = 0.9332$.)
steps: We could not do this for a single worker: one commute is skewed, not normal. The CLT applies to the mean.

blocks.title: Too small a sample
blocks.q: Could you use the normal model for the mean of just 4 commutes?
steps: With n = 4 from a strongly skewed population, $\bar{x}$ is still noticeably skewed.
Its mean (30) and SD ($12/2 = 6$) are still correct, but normal-curve probabilities would be off.
blocks.a: No: the shape is not yet close to normal.

blocks.html: Thinking the central limit theorem makes the data normal. A large sample from a skewed population looks skewed, like the population. The theorem is about the distribution of $\bar{x}$ over many samples. Check: are you describing individual values (population shape) or sample means (approximately normal for large n)?
The econometrics probability chapter lets you watch averages of lopsided data pile up into a bell, and builds every regression test on this theorem.
